newsitem.title: USA: Clinton activism could rise in second term.
newsitem.headline: Clinton activism could rise in second term.

text.p: U.N. Ambassador Madeleine Albright predicted on Thursday that President Bill Clinton will be more of an activist on foreign policy if he is elected to a second term.

"What I would see him doing is taking up the opportunities that have been presented by the major shifts in a post-Cold War era and making sure that that 'indispensable' aspect of America's role and power is visible," she told a meeting of Overseas Writers, a group of foreign policy journalists.
This would suggest "much more involvement in terms of an activist way of seeing the United States working to solve some of the problems that are out there," she said.

Albright, the Clinton administration's envoy to the United Nations, is among the leading candidates being discussed for Secretary of State if Clinton wins re-election on Nov. 5 and if Secretary of State Warren Christopher leaves that post.

A long-time Democratic activist and foreign policy adviser to leading party officials, she stressed the importance of having a president who "sees the United States looking outward rather than inward ... and one who builds on the fact that we are moving into the 21st century rather than that the Second World War is over."

This last comment echoed a Clinton campaign theme aimed at faulting Republican challenger Bob Dole for repeatedly harkening back to his Second World War military experiences and to that era as a better time.

Albright, asked to name some specific issues Clinton would focus on in a second term, cited managing key U.S. ties with Russia and engaging more with China, "probably the most important (relationship) we have coming up in the 21st century."
She also cited paying more attention to U.S. ties to Europe, "working very hard to understand the importance of regional conflicts to us," and more dealings with Asia as a whole.

Albright, an advocate of strong U.S. international leadership, believes the United States, as the sole remaining superpower, is an "indispensable country" on the world stage and "must assert where the intervention of the United States would assist in making a better world."

But she stressed that "we are not out there simply to bully people around or to decide that we can deal with every conceivable problem in the world. We have to choose what issues are important to us and when to use what type of power."

Although the post-Cold War era is more complicated and poses much different threats, there are now more tools for the United States to use -- including the United Nations, sanctions, peacekeeping and military forces -- "to calibrate our response" to the myriad challenges, she said.

"I'm probably the greatest defender of American power that there is but even I understand that we can't do everything," added Albright, who is credited with making one of the most compelling arguments for U.S. involvement in Bosnia during internal administration debates.
